title: Scholarship & learning
summary: The scholar self-extends through knowledge—and can converse with people, the universe, and natural laws.

sections.heading: Knowledge as extension
sections.body:
The scholar defines self-extension as an expansion of their mental faculties and knowledge. The language used here can be English, Spanish, Chinese, Arabic, anything. Or it could be mathematical symbols and programming languages. The scholar can converse with others, or the scholar can converse with the universe and natural laws. Either way, the scholar self-extends.

Academically, the more vocabulary—jargon—you learn from different fields, the more people and researchers you can communicate with. A formula that once meant nothing becomes something you can read. Learning its language gives you access to a relationship you could not describe before.

If someone was unable to communicate in any manner with anything, how might they self-extend? The very nature of self-extension requires something other than the self. And you access ideas, people, and things outside yourself through language.

question: Who can now participate in a conversation that was previously closed to them?

title: Wealth & influence
summary: The CEO defines self-extension as an accumulation of influence through wealth and power.

sections.heading: An expanding sphere of influence
sections.body:
The CEO defines self-extension as an accumulation of influence—extension—through wealth and power. Some people have a lust for power as their form of self-extension: it is what gives them self-worth.

We often ask people, “What makes you happy?” Maybe we should be asking them if their basic needs are fulfilled, and then beyond that, their definition of self-extension. And from your definition of self-extension comes your version of self-worth.

This brings us back to pain and pleasure. Money can relieve the pain of not having your basic needs met. But if your definition of success is always having more, when does that pursuit stop bringing relief? Horace’s Satire 1.1 raises a related question about wanting more and remaining dissatisfied (Horace, n.d.).

You can also examine someone’s language for what they do not have to say to see how powerful they are. Who can give a command and expect to be understood? Who does not have to flatter or please others? Influence changes the work a person can leave to everyone else.

question: Is this ambition enlarging a life, or making contentment permanently unreachable?

title: Travel
summary: The traveler defines self-extension as a physical extension.

sections.heading: Beyond the immediate surroundings
sections.body:
The traveler defines self-extension as a physical extension. Once our basic physical needs are met, we begin to want to extend ourselves beyond our immediate physical surroundings—beyond our room.

But reaching another place also brings us back to language. Literally, the more languages you understand, the more people you understand. The more people you have met and talked with, the more circumstances you have encountered. You can communicate and empathize better with people you meet in the future because you might have seen similar circumstances.

Conversely, think about English speakers expecting to go other places and have other people speak English to them. They are not the ones forced to learn another language. Who has to do the work of making this encounter possible?

question: Does this encounter expand understanding on both sides?

title: Religion & spirituality
summary: Self-extension can be spiritual: communication with something beyond the immediately visible world.

sections.heading: A spiritual horizon
sections.body:
Self-extension can be mental, physical, material, spiritual—anything. The priest might define self-extension as communication with a higher power and an expansion of consciousness. The communication, the language, is with that higher power, whatever that may be in the priest’s religion or belief system.

I am not religious, and this is a secular perspective, so correct me if I am wrong. I do not mean that every religion defines the self or its purpose in the same way. The question is how someone understands their own connection to something beyond themselves.

What does that connection make possible for them? As with the scholar, the traveler, or the lover, I would begin by asking what their definition of self-extension is.

question: How does this person describe their own spiritual form of self-extension?

title: Love & relationships
summary: You experience the world both through your own eyes and through theirs.

sections.heading: A self that includes another
sections.body:
The lover sees their significant other as a part of themselves—self-extension. You experience the world both through your own eyes and through theirs. This also applies platonically; the romantic version is just what we usually think about.

This is why people say communication is key, communication is key, communication is key. A relationship expects equal footing, so you cannot try to hold all the power and expect the other person to guess what you are feeling, get mad when they do not, and say it is their obligation to.

Language is power in what you can do, but power also shows up in what you do not have to do. If one person always has to explain and the other expects to be understood, whose feelings are doing all the work?

Use your words. Give the other person something they can understand and respond to, and listen to theirs. Experiencing the world through another person’s eyes still means allowing them to have a perspective of their own.

question: Where am I asking to be understood without helping someone understand?

title: Illness & the shrinking world
summary: Pain reduces one’s world and reverses self-extension.

sections.heading: When the world contracts
sections.body:
I understand pain, following Scarry, as the antithesis to language. Scarry posits that pain undoes self-extension, reducing your world back to your immediate physical surroundings (Scarry, 1985).

Nothing else matters: you are in pain. Your money, travels, and mathematical formulas do not help right now. A little dramatic—but imagine the last time you had a fever or got severely ill, lying in bed, confined to your room. Ideas from your civilization are usurped by that migraine.

This is all to say that pain reduces one’s world and reverses self-extension. The things that usually make your world feel large can become distant when your body demands all your attention.

If relief makes room to reach outward again, then asking whether someone’s basic needs are fulfilled comes before asking how they want to self-extend. What would make their immediate world more bearable? What do they want to be able to reach again?

question: What would give this person room to attend to the world again?

title: Pedagogy
summary: School should do three things at minimum: teach academic excellence, emotional intelligence, and moral reasoning.

sections.heading: Three tasks of education
sections.body:
Teachers are so important. I have thought about this a lot: school should do three things at minimum.

How does this tie into language? Each gives students a way to access something outside themselves: knowledge, people whose lives differ from theirs, and a vocabulary for understanding how people treat one another.

Horace says in Sermones 1.4 that his father “dictis formabat”—he was shaping me with his words. His father teaches through examples, and Horace goes on to examine his own conduct. This is what schools should do: give students words and examples they can carry into their own lives (Horace, n.d.).

items.title: Academic excellence
items.body: Obviously: how to learn, acquire knowledge, and so on. This is what we think of school as doing by default.

items.title: Emotional intelligence
items.body: How to communicate with others. If you only understand how to communicate with a small, bubbled subset of the population, what happens when you meet people outside it? A narrow social environment can leave someone unprepared to understand people with different circumstances. School should give students opportunities to reach beyond that bubble.

items.title: Moral reasoning
items.body: This is especially important for kids who observe inverted morals at home, including abuse—one form or another of inducing pain. Teaching can mean literally showing kids what is wrong and what is right: showing an example of embezzlement and labeling it “embezzlement,” doing the same with abuse, or showing positive examples such as a healthy friendship or relationship. Give students language for recognizing what they are seeing.

question: What experience could a student recognize and communicate after this lesson?

title: Politics & rhetoric
summary: Denying that an event caused pain can prevent healing and cause more pain.

sections.heading: The power to frame an event
sections.body:
If you observe political speeches, you might see different events being framed with different words and rhetoric. For example, torture being framed as not torture. Denying that an event caused pain can prevent healing, which causes more pain. This obstructs justice and prevents self-extension because, again, pain is world-destroying.

Conversely, power is language: what you do not have to do. English speakers might expect to go other places and have other people speak English to them. They are not the ones forced to learn another language.

Consider a country that commits war crimes in another country, and a court that conducts the trials in the perpetrator’s language. This is an example of the question I want to ask: who can manipulate their own vocabulary, and who has to translate their experience into someone else’s terms? The language in which harm is acknowledged can itself become an obstacle to healing.

When examining people and institutions, I can apply the model and see if there is a plausible explanation for why somebody, some company, or some country took a certain action. What type of language were they fed? What type of language are they putting out there to achieve what effect?

question: Whose account of what happened is allowed to define the situation?

title: Violence
summary: Examine the pain that is preexisting, the pain an action causes, and the pain that persists afterwards.

sections.heading: Force, power, and harm
sections.body:
My thoughts on violence run in parallel with my thoughts on language. One way I understand violence on an individual level is as a physical manifestation—in a sense, communication—of overwhelming internal emotions, often pain.

Language exists as a foil because, with similar vocabulary on both the speaking and receiving end, overwhelming sensation can at least in part be communicated. From my perspective, relieving the mental pain of an incommunicable feeling may help interrupt one route to violence.

So when I consider problems relating to violence, I come from a perspective of examining the pain that is preexisting, the pain that it causes, and the pain that persists afterwards. When I consider language, I can look at it from two perspectives: causing pain and relieving it. There is this duality.

This is one possible route to violence, rather than an explanation of every act. Violence can also be deliberate: force or power used to injure, threaten, or deprive another person (Krug et al., 2002). Understanding someone’s pain does not excuse the harm they cause. The pain carried by the person harmed must remain part of the account.

question: What pain preceded this action, and who is now carrying its consequences?

title: Incel culture & dominance
summary: What happens when expressing emotion is dismissed and displays of dominance are what matter?

sections.heading: A narrowed vocabulary
sections.body:
Think about the social media version of incel culture: people are taught that language—explicitly, expressing your emotions—does not matter, and that displays of dominance, violence, and inducing pain are what matter. This is evidently problematic.

If someone is lonely or hurt but is taught that saying so is weakness, what ways do they have left to communicate it? A community can give someone language for their feelings, or it can reward turning those feelings into blame and dominance.

The pain is worth hearing. It does not entitle someone to another person’s attention or affection. The question is what kind of language a community gives people for understanding rejection, and what actions that language encourages.

question: What ways of expressing vulnerability does this community make possible?

title: Misunderstanding
summary: Misunderstandings in dramas: avoidable, devastating, and a reminder to use your words.

sections.heading: The missing explanation
sections.body:
Misunderstandings in dramas can be so avoidable and so devastating. Someone does not explain what they mean, the other person guesses, and everything that follows rests on a feeling that never became shared knowledge.

A relationship expects equal footing. You cannot expect the other person to guess what you are feeling and then get mad when they do not. What do they actually know? What are they filling in for themselves?

I always think it is funny when a child has learned some basic words and still whines for what they want, and the parent says, “Use your words.” It is applicable to more than just these children. Use your words. Look at others’ words to understand their worlds.

Of course, understanding each other does not mean agreeing on everything. But at least then the conversation can be about what each person means, instead of an explanation neither person has checked.

question: Which part of the conflict rests on an assumption nobody has checked?

title: Bullying & silencing
summary: Being hurt and then told to keep quiet leaves pain with nowhere to go.

sections.heading: Pain without an audience
sections.body:
Bullying, the quiet kid, “hurt people hurt people”: I keep coming back to what happens when someone is hurt and then told to keep quiet. They may never have been taught to deal with what was happening or to communicate their emotions through language.

In the model, overwhelming feeling that cannot be communicated can become one route to further harm. This does not mean that being bullied makes someone violent, or that responsibility for later harm disappears. It means we should ask what happens to pain when every attempt to express it is shut down.

Telling someone to use their words only helps if someone else will listen. Who hears them when they describe what happened? Does speaking lead to help, or are they punished for it? Addressing the bullying itself is part of giving those words somewhere to go.

question: Who can hear this person without dismissing or punishing their account?

title: Parenting
summary: The balance lies between not communicating at all and communicating through constant control.

sections.heading: Two limiting cases
sections.body:
The two extremes are parents who do not communicate or talk to their children at all and leave them to their own devices, and parents who communicate or control too much. The balance is somewhere in between.

Language can give a child a way to understand what is happening and express what they feel. But power also shows up in the expectation of being understood without having to explain. A parent can give a command and punish a child for not complying. What room does the child have to ask why?

If the goal is to help someone self-extend, then the question is what your words make possible for them. Are you giving them ways to learn, communicate, and reason for themselves? Or does every decision still depend on you?

question: Are these words helping a child develop their own capacity to understand and act?

title: Abuse & obstructed agency
summary: Someone can respond to frustration in their own self-extension by preventing someone else from extending.

sections.heading: Blocking another person’s extension
sections.body:
One pattern I see in abuse is somebody being hindered from self-extending and, instead of dealing with their own problems, choosing to prevent others from self-extending.

This is a way to examine a pattern, not a complete explanation of abuse. Look at whose world is being reduced: who can maintain friendships, pursue an ambition, speak freely, or make a decision without permission?

Power is also language in what someone does not have to say. One person can expect to be understood and obeyed, while the other has to keep explaining, reassuring, or pleasing them. The unequal work of communication can help reveal the control.

The responsibility belongs to the person causing harm. Someone being controlled does not have an obligation to find the perfect words to make it stop.

question: Whose ability to connect, choose, or speak is being restricted?

title: Art & expression
summary: Dance, art, writing: language can become self-extension and a way toward relief.

sections.heading: Language beyond speech
sections.body:
Art—dance, visual art, writing—is language. It can be self-extension and a way toward healing: a feeling becomes something outside yourself, something you can move through, look at, or share.

If language is broadly communication, then it does not have to begin as speech. The important thing is that an overwhelming sensation can at least in part be communicated. A movement or an image may give it a form that an ordinary explanation has not.

You access ideas, people, and things outside yourself through language. Making something can be one way to reach outward; encountering someone else’s art can be another. What can this form communicate, and who can understand it?

question: What can this form express that ordinary speech has not been able to carry?

title: Learning & association
summary: Experience shapes what we expect, what we approach, and what we avoid.

sections.heading: Learning what to expect
sections.body:
Classical conditioning concerns learning relationships between events. A cue that predicts an outcome can come to elicit a response of its own. Within this model, that helps explain how a word, place, or tone of voice could come to signal anticipated pain or comfort (Spielman et al., 2020).

It helps to distinguish a cue from a consequence in the same example. A particular tone of voice might predict an argument and bring anxiety before a conversation begins. Leaving the room might then reduce that anxiety. The first relationship concerns what predicts what; the second concerns what follows an action and whether that result makes the action more likely.

Operant conditioning concerns actions and their consequences. Reinforcement increases a behavior; punishment decreases it. Avoiding a conversation may remove anxiety. If that relief makes future avoidance more likely, this is negative reinforcement. Relief now can coexist with an unresolved problem later (Spielman et al., 2020).

Synaptic plasticity includes changes in the strength of connections between neurons and contributes to learning and memory. Some dopamine signals track differences between expected and received rewards. These mechanisms help us examine how experience shapes behavior, without proving that the entire model describes every action (O’Doherty, 2011; Purves et al., 2001).

A response learned in one situation can continue when the circumstances change. Avoidance that once reduced a real threat may later interrupt a conversation that could be manageable. The useful distinction is between what the response accomplished before and what its consequences are now.

This gives the broader model a way to examine why a response persists. Something can continue to feel necessary because it has repeatedly produced immediate relief, even when its later effects are costly. Asking about the learned expectation and the present consequence can reveal different parts of the pattern without reducing a person’s whole life to a single mechanism.

question: What did this response help you avoid or obtain before, and what does it do now?
